toc.title: Three signs you're grounded in safety

sections.title: 1. Can you notice your sensory experience?
3. Do you feel an impulse to connect?

blocks.p: Accessing your safety state is different from coping with emotional dysregulation. Here I want to look at the difference, and at how you can use both.

How do you recognize actual safety, as different from less danger? What's the difference between "I'm grounded in my safety state" and "I feel less crummy," or "I feel less defensive"? Am I actually grounded in safety, or am I just reducing my stuck defensive state, my dysregulation?
I call that second one coping. So it's anchoring versus coping.

In therapy, a lot of what we do, with a very behavioral kind of focus, is about how you deal with things when they come up. I would call that coping. There's some overlap, obviously. Maybe you're using a safety anchor to cope, and that's fine. But there's a difference between "I'm grounded in my safety state" and "I'm getting through the moment," even though they can overlap.

blocks.h: Three signs you're grounded in safety

blocks.p: There are three big indicators for me.

blocks.h3: 1. Can you notice your sensory experience?

blocks.p: The first one is: are you actually able to notice your sensory experience? If you can be mindful enough to notice what your senses are telling you, that tells me you're pretty grounded in your safety state. You're grounded enough.

Holding an ice cube, not to calm yourself but to distract yourself, isn't really mindfully experiencing a sense. It might be effective for not self-harming, and that's great. But it's a lot different from slowing down, taking in a sense, and really noticing how it affects you. Those are different kinds of anchoring. With one, you're getting through the moment. With the other, you're really experiencing the moment.

The second big indicator: do you feel curiosity? If you're feeling desperation, "I want this to end, and I'm going to do whatever I can, all the coping skills I've learned," that's great. You can do that. Nothing wrong with that at all. Please do that. But it doesn't necessarily involve curiosity. That's more like flight or fight, maybe a little freeze. That's desperation: I want this to stop, I want it to go away.
Versus: what's it like for me to do (fill in the blank)? What is the experience for me of playing with this fidget? I'm really curious how this impacts me.

That's curiosity. If you're able to be curious, that tells me you're pretty well anchored in your safety state. If you want something to go away, if you want a feeling to stop, that tells me you're probably more in a defensive state.

We want to come at the defensive states with curiosity. So being able to stay anchored in your safety state should be well established first. Then you can come at your defensive states with curiosity and ask yourself: what's it like to be me? What is it like for me to experience this stuck defensive state? Not to make it go away, but to actually experience it.

Deb Dana said it well on the podcast: "When we begin to take away some of that judgment, that self-criticism, then there's room for curiosity. And curiosity is what you need in order to befriend." ([Episode 29](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c))

blocks.h3: 3. Do you feel an impulse to connect?

blocks.p: The third one is how strong your impulse to connect is. All of our different polyvagal states have impulses. From safety, the impulse is to connect: with others, and/or with the self.

So when I'm in my safety state, I'm way more likely to go and play with my kids, or give my wife a hug, or talk to my coworkers, which I don't usually like to do. Even in my safety state, I do pretty darn well when I'm alone. So when I have the impulse to go connect with my coworkers, I know I must be pretty well grounded in my safety state.

If you're curious about what's happening inside of you, and you have an impulse to just pause and breathe, that tells me you're connected to the self. It tells me you're able to access your curiosity, your sensory experience, and even your internal world. All of that is a really good indicator that you're grounded enough in your safety state.
That's way different from "I want this frustration to go away. What's wrong with me? How do I stop this? What's the coping skill I'm supposed to use to make this go away?"

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: I think it's totally okay to just cope, deal with it, and get through the moment. It's not easy to transition from there, especially if you haven't practiced, or you don't have the vagal brake strength developed yet. It can be really hard to go from coping to mindful experiencing, curiosity, and being in a safety state, especially without co-regulation. I can do that in therapy with people, because they have co-regulation and I'm walking them through it. On your own, that's quite a challenge.

So I think it's completely okay to separate the two: "I'm just dealing with the situation right now. I'm simply dealing with it. When I'm ready, I'll come back to this. Maybe I'll take a break, do some more safety anchoring, and then come back and allow myself to become more curious about the inner experience I was going through earlier."
It's okay to gap those out. I don't expect people to go from dysregulation to coping and then straight to mindful experiencing. That can be quite a challenge.
